L9: # Title:YAPA: A generic tool for computing intruder knowledge
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Mathieu Baudet】, 【6†Véronique Cortier】, 【7†Stéphanie Delaune】

L16: > Abstract:Reasoning about the knowledge of an attacker is a necessary step in many formal analyses of security protocols. In the framework of the applied pi calculus, as in similar languages based on equational logics, knowledge is typically expressed by two relations: deducibility and static equivalence. Several decision procedures have been proposed for these relations under a variety of equational theories. However, each theory has its particular algorithm, and none has been implemented so far.
L17: We provide a generic procedure for deducibility and static equivalence that takes as input any convergent rewrite system. We show that our algorithm covers most of the existing decision procedures for convergent theories. We also provide an efficient implementation, and compare it briefly with the tools ProVerif and KiSs.

L0@P0: DEEPSEC: Deciding Equivalence Properties in Security Protocols
L1@P0: Theory and Practice
L2@P0: Vincent Cheval, Steve Kremer, Itsaka Rakotonirina
L3@P0: Inria & LORIA
L4@P0: Abstract—Automated verification has become an essential part
L5@P0: in the security evaluation of cryptographic protocols. Recently,
L6@P0: there has been a considerable effort to lift the theory and
L7@P0: tool support that existed for reachability properties to the
L8@P0: more complex case of equivalence properties. In this paper
L9@P0: we contribute both to the theory and practice of this verification problem. We establish new complexity results for
L10@P0: static equivalence, trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity
L11@P0: and provide a decision procedure for these equivalences in
L12@P0: the case of a bounded number of sessions. Our procedure is
L13@P0: the first to decide trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity
L14@P0: exactly for a large variety of cryptographic primitives—those
L15@P0: that can be represented by a subterm convergent destructor
L16@P0: rewrite system. We implemented the procedure in a new tool,
L17@P0: DEEPSEC. We showed through extensive experiments that it
L18@P0: is significantly more efficient than other similar tools, while at
L19@P0: the same time raises the scope of the protocols that can be
L20@P0: analysed.
L21@P0: 1. Introduction
L22@P0: The use of automated, formal methods has become
L23@P0: indispensable for analysing complex security protocols, such
L24@P0: as those for authentication, key exchange and secure channel
L25@P0: establishment. Nowadays there exist mature, fully automated
L26@P0: such analysers; among others AVISPA [11], ProVerif [17],
L27@P0: Scyther [33], Tamarin [45] or Maude-NPA [44]. These tools
L28@P0: operate in so-called symbolic models, rooted in the seminal
L29@P0: work by Dolev and Yao [35]: the attacker has full control
L30@P0: of the communication network, unbounded computational
L31@P0: power, but cryptography is idealised. This model is well
L32@P0: suited for finding attacks in the protocol logic, and tools have
L33@P0: indeed been extremely effective in discovering this kind of
L34@P0: flaw or proving their absence.
L35@P0: While most works investigate reachability properties, a
L36@P0: recent trend consists in adapting the tools—and the underlying theory—for the more complex indistinguishability
L37@P0: properties. Such properties are generally modelled as a
L38@P0: behavioural equivalence (bisimulation or trace equivalence)
L39@P0: in a dedicated process calculus such as the Spi [6] or applied
L40@P0: pi calculus [5]. A typical example is real-or-random secrecy:
L41@P0: after interacting with a protocol, an adversary is unable
L42@P0: to distinguish the real secret used in the protocol from a
L43@P0: random value. Privacy-type properties can also be expressed
L44@P0: as such: anonymity may be modeled as the adversary’s
L45@P0: inability to distinguish two instances of a protocol executed
L46@P0: by different agents; vote privacy [34] has been expressed as
L47@P0: indistinguishability of the situations where the votes of two
L48@P0: agents have been swapped or not; unlinkability [8] is seen
L49@P0: as indistinguishability of two sessions, either both executed
L50@P0: by the same agent A, or by two different agents A and B.
L51@P0: Related work. The problem of analysing security protocols
L52@P0: is undecidable in general but several decidable subclasses
L53@P0: have been identified. While many complexity results are
L54@P0: known for trace properties [36], [42], the case of behavioural
L55@P0: equivalences remains mostly open. When the attacker is
L56@P0: an eavesdropper and cannot interact with the protocol, the
L57@P0: indistinguishability problem—static equivalence—has been
L58@P0: shown PTIME for large classes of cryptographic primitives [3], [27], [29]. For active attackers, bounding the
L59@P0: number of protocol sessions is often sufficient to obtain
L60@P0: decidability [42] and is of practical interest: most real-life
L61@P0: attacks indeed only require a small number of sessions.
L62@P0: In this context Baudet [14], and later Chevalier and Rusinowtich [24], showed that real-or-random secrecy was coNP
L63@P0: for cryptographic primitives that can be modelled as subterm convergent rewrite systems, by checking whether two
L64@P0: constraint systems admit the same set of solutions. These
L65@P0: procedures do however not allow for else branches, nor
L66@P0: do they verify trace equivalence in full generality. In [23],
L67@P0: Cheval et al. have used Baudet’s procedure as a black box to
L68@P0: verify trace equivalence of determinate processes. This class
L69@P0: of processes is however insufficient for most anonymity
L70@P0: properties. Finally, decidability results for an unbounded
L71@P0: number of sessions were proposed in [26], [25], but with
L72@P0: severe restrictions on processes and equational theories.
L73@P0: Tool support also exists for verifying equivalence properties. We start discussing tools that are limited to a bounded
L74@P0: number of sessions. The SPEC tool [46], [47] verifies a
L75@P0: sound symbolic bisimulation, but is restricted to particular
L76@P0: cryptographic primitives (pairing, encryption, signatures and
L77@P0: hash functions) and does not allow for else branches. The
L78@P0: APTE tool [20] covers the same primitives but allows else
L79@P0: branches and decides trace equivalence exactly. On the
L80@P0: contrary, the AKISS tool [19] allows for user-defined cryptographic primitives. Partial correctness of AKISS is shown
L81@P0: for primitives modelled by an arbitrary convergent rewrite
L82@P0: system that has the finite variant property [28]. Termination
L83@P0-1: is additionally shown for subterm convergent rewrite systems. However, AKISS does only decide trace equivalencefor a class of determinate processes; for other processes
L84@P1: trace equivalence can be both over- and under-approximated
L85@P1: which proved to be sufficient on many examples. The recent
L86@P1: SAT-EQUIV tool [30] uses a different approach: it relies on
L87@P1: Graph Planning and SAT solving to verify trace equivalence,
L88@P1: rather than a dedicated procedure. The tool is extremely
L89@P1: efficient and several orders of magnitude faster than other
L90@P1: tools. It does however not guarantee termination and is
L91@P1: currently restricted to pairing and symmetric encryption
L92@P1: and only considers a class of simple processes (a subclass
L93@P1: of determinate processes) that satisfy a type-compliance
L94@P1: condition. These restrictions severely limit its scope.
L95@P1: Other tools support verification of equivalence properties, even for an unbounded number of sessions. This
L96@P1: is the case of ProVerif [15], Tamarin [13] and Maude
L97@P1: NPA [44] which all allow for user-defined cryptographic
L98@P1: primitives. However, given that the underlying problem is
L99@P1: undecidable, these tools may not terminate. Moreover, they
L100@P1: only approximate trace equivalence by verifying the more
L101@P1: fine-grained diff-equivalence. This equivalence is too finegrained on many examples. While some recent improvements on ProVerif [21], [16] helps covering more protocols,
L102@P1: general verification of trace equivalence is still out of scope.
L103@P1: For instance, the verification by Arapinis et al. [10] of
L104@P1: unlinkability in the 3G mobile phone protocols required
L105@P1: some “tricks” and approximations of the protocol to avoid
L106@P1: false attacks. In [31], Cortier et al. develop a type system and
L107@P1: automated type checker for verifying equivalences. While
L108@P1: extremely efficient, this tool only covers a fixed set of
L109@P1: cryptographic primitives (the same as SPEC and APTE) and
L110@P1: verifies an approximated equivalence, similar to the diffequivalence. A different approach has been taken by Hirschi
L111@P1: et al. [38], identifying sufficient conditions provable by
L112@P1: ProVerif for verifying unlinkability properties, implemented
L113@P1: in the tool Ukano, a front-end to the ProVerif tool. Ukano
L114@P1: does however not verify equivalence properties in general.
L115@P1: Contributions. We significantly improve the theoretical
L116@P1: understanding and the practical verification of equivalence
L117@P1: when the number of protocol sessions is bounded. We
L118@P1: emphasise that even in this setting, the system under study
L119@P1: has an infinite state space due to the term algebra modelling
L120@P1: cryptographic primitives. Our work targets the wide class of
L121@P1: cryptographic primitives that can be represented by a subterm convergent rewriting system. Concretely, we provide
L122@P1: 1) new tight complexity results for static equivalence (∼),
L123@P1: trace equivalence (≈t) and labelled bisimilarity (≈`);
L124@P1: 2) a novel procedure for deciding trace equivalence and
L125@P1: labelled bisimilarity for the class of cryptographic
L126@P1: primitives modelled by a destructor subterm convergent
L127@P1: rewrite system;
L128@P1: 3) an implementation of our procedure for trace equivalence in a new tool called DEEPSEC (DEciding Equivalence Properties for SECurity protocols).
L129@P1: We detail the three contributions below.
L130@P1: Complexity. We provide the first complexity results for
L131@P1: deciding trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity in the
L132@P1: applied pi calculus, without any restriction on the class of
L133@P1: protocols (other than bounding the number of sessions).
L134@P1: In particular, our results are not restricted to determinate
L135@P1: processes, allow for else branches and do not approximate
L136@P1: equivalence. Let us also highlight one small, yet substantial
L137@P1: difference with existing work: we do not consider cryptographic primitives (rewrite systems) as constants of the
L138@P1: problem. As most modern verification tools allow for userspecified primitives [17], [45], [44], [19], our approach
L139@P1: seems to better fit this reality. Typically, all existing procedures for static equivalence can only be claimed PTIME
L140@P1: because of this difference and are actually exponential in
L141@P1: the sizes of signature or equational theory. Our complexity
L142@P1: results are summarised in fig. 1. All our lower bounds hold
L143@P1: for subterm convergent rewrite systems (destructor or not)
L144@P1: and even for the positive fragment (without else branches).
L145@P1: En passant, we present results for the pi calculus1: although
L146@P1: investigated in [18], complexity was unknown when restricted to a bounded number of sessions. Still, our main
L147@P1: result is the coNEXP completeness (and in particular, the
L148@P1: decidability) of trace equivalence and labelled bisimilarity
L149@P1: for destructor subterm convergent rewrite systems.
L150@P1: Pure pi calculus Applied pi calculus

L153@P1: ≈t Π2 complete coNEXP complete

L156@P1: Decision procedure. We present a novel procedure based
L157@P1: on a symbolic semantics and constraint solving. Unlike most
L158@P1: other work, our procedure decides equivalences exactly, i.e.
L159@P1: without approximations. Moreover, it does not restrict the
L160@P1: class of processes (except for replication), nor the use of
L161@P1: else branches, and is correct for any cryptographic primitives
L162@P1: that can be modelled by a subterm convergent destructor
L163@P1: rewrite system (see section 2). The design of the procedure
L164@P1: did greatly benefit from our complexity study, and was
L165@P1: developed in order to obtain tight complexity upper bounds.

L16: > Abstract:Formal methods have proved effective to automatically analyze protocols. Over the past years, much research has focused on verifying trace equivalence on protocols, which is notably used to model many interesting privacy properties, e.g., anonymity or unlinkability. Many tools for checking trace equivalence rely on a naive and expensive exploration of all interleavings of concurrent actions, which calls for partial-order reduction (POR) techniques.
L17: In this paper, we present the first POR technique for protocol equivalences that does not rely on an action-determinism assumption: we recast the trace equivalence problem as a reachability problem, to which persistent and sleep set techniques can be applied, and we show how to effectively apply these results in the context of symbolic executions. We report on a prototype implementation, improving the tool DeepSec.
